Chandogya Upanishad.question: The symbolic legend then presents conversation of _____ with a bull, a fire, a swan (Hamsa, हंस) and a diver bird (Madgu, मद्गु), which respectively are symbolism for Vayu, Agni, Āditya and Prāṇa
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The sage sends Satyakama to tend four hundred cows, and come back when they multiply into a thousand. The symbolic legend then presents conversation of Satyakama with a bull, a fire, a swan (Hamsa, हंस) and a diver bird (Madgu, मद्गु), which respectively are symbolism for Vayu, Agni, Āditya and Prāṇa.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Satyakama returns to his teacher with a thousand cows, and humbly learns the rest of the nature of _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Satyakama then learns from these creatures that forms of Brahman is in all cardinal directions (north, south, east, west), world-bodies (earth, atmosphere, sky and ocean), sources of light (fire, Sun, Moon, lightning), and in man (breath, eye, ear and mind). Satyakama returns to his teacher with a thousand cows, and humbly learns the rest of the nature of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The story is notable for declaring that the mark of a student of _____ is not parentage, but honesty
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Satyakama then learns from these creatures that forms of Brahman is in all cardinal directions (north, south, east, west), world-bodies (earth, atmosphere, sky and ocean), sources of light (fire, Sun, Moon, lightning), and in man (breath, eye, ear and mind). Satyakama returns to his teacher with a thousand cows, and humbly learns the rest of the nature of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The story is also notable for the repeated use of the word _____ to mean teacher during the Vedic era
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The story is also notable for the repeated use of the word Bhagavan to mean teacher during the Vedic era.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The boy _____ described in volumes 4.4 through 4.9 of the text, is declared to be the grown up Guru (teacher) with whom Upakosala has been studying for twelve years in his Brahmacharya
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The boy Satyakama Jabala described in volumes 4.4 through 4.9 of the text, is declared to be the grown up Guru (teacher) with whom Upakosala has been studying for twelve years in his Brahmacharya.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The fires then enumerate the manifestations of _____ to be everywhere in the empirically perceived world
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Upakosala has a conversation with sacrificial fires, which inform him that Brahman is life, Brahman is joy and bliss, Brahman is infinity, and the means to Brahman is not through depressing, hard penance. The fires then enumerate the manifestations of Brahman to be everywhere in the empirically perceived world.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: "He is the immortal free from fear; he is _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Upakosala has a conversation with sacrificial fires, which inform him that Brahman is life, Brahman is joy and bliss, Brahman is infinity, and the means to Brahman is not through depressing, hard penance. The fires then enumerate the manifestations of Brahman to be everywhere in the empirically perceived world.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The Upanishad asserts in verses 4.15.2 and 4.15.3 that the _____ is the "stronghold of love", the leader of love, and that it assembles and unites all that inspires love
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Satyakama joins Upakosala's education and explains, in volume 4.15 of the text, य एषोऽक्षिणि पुरुषो दृश्यत एष आत्मेति होवाचैतदमृतमभयमेतद्ब्रह्मेति The person you see here in the eye — he is the [S]elf (atman)" he told him. The Upanishad asserts in verses 4.15.2 and 4.15.3 that the Atman is the "stronghold of love", the leader of love, and that it assembles and unites all that inspires love.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Those who find and realize the Atman, find and realize the _____, states the text
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: "He is the immortal free from fear; he is Brahman. Those who find and realize the Atman, find and realize the Brahman, states the text.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: They ask their father, _____, as who is the noblest and best among them
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: They ask their father, Prajapati, as who is the noblest and best among them. Prajapati states, "he by whose departure, the body is worst off, is the one".

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Then, _____ (breath, life-principle) prepares to leave, and all of them insist that he stay
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Then, Prana (breath, life-principle) prepares to leave, and all of them insist that he stay. Prana, they acknowledge, empowers them all.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: These sections are nearly identical to those found in section 14.9.1 of Sathapatha Brahmana, in section 6.2 of _____, and in chapter 1 of Kaushitaki Upanishad
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: These sections are nearly identical to those found in section 14.9.1 of Sathapatha Brahmana, in section 6.2 of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and in chapter 1 of Kaushitaki Upanishad.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The two paths of after-life, states the text, are _____ – the path of the Devas (gods), and Pitryana – the path of the fathers
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The two paths of after-life, states the text, are Devayana – the path of the Devas (gods), and Pitryana – the path of the fathers.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: One, it adds a third way for tiny living creatures (flies, insects, worms) that neither take the _____ nor the Pitryana path after their death
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: One, it adds a third way for tiny living creatures (flies, insects, worms) that neither take the Devayana nor the Pitryana path after their death.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: When the knowledge seekers arrive, the king pays his due respect to them, gives them gifts, but the five ask him about _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: When the knowledge seekers arrive, the king pays his due respect to them, gives them gifts, but the five ask him about Vaisvanara Self.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The answer that follows is referred to as the "doctrine of _____", where Vaisvanara literally means "One in the Many"
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The adults are described as five great householders and great theologians who once came together and held a discussion as to what is our Self, and what is Brahman? The five householders approach a sage named Uddalaka Aruni, who admits his knowledge is deficient, and suggests that they all go to king Asvapati Kaikeya, who knows about Atman Vaishvanara. The answer that follows is called the "doctrine of Atman Vaishvanara", where Vaisvanara literally means "One in the Many".

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The entire doctrine is also found in other ancient Indian texts such as the _____ (section 10.6.1)
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The entire doctrine is also found in other ancient Indian texts such as the Satapatha Brahmana (section 10.6.1).

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The common essence of the theory, as found in various ancient _____ texts, is that "the inner fire, the Self, is universal and common in all men, whether they are friends or foe, good or bad"
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The entire doctrine is also found in other ancient Indian texts such as the Satapatha Brahmana (section 10.6.1). The common essence of the theory, as found in various ancient Indian texts, is that "the inner fire, the Self, is universal and common in all men, whether they are friends or foe, good or bad".

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The Chandogya narrative is notable for stating the idea of unity of the _____, of realization of this unity within man, and that there is unity and oneness in all beings
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The Chandogya narrative is notable for stating the idea of unity of the Universe, of realization of this unity within man, and that there is unity and oneness in all beings.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: This idea of universal oneness of all Selfs, seeing others as oneself, seeing _____ as Atman and Atman as Brahman, became a foundational premise for Vedanta theologians
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The entire doctrine is also found in other ancient Indian texts such as the Satapatha Brahmana (section 10.6.1). This idea of universal oneness of all Selfs, seeing others as oneself, seeing Brahman as Atman and Atman as Brahman, became a foundational premise for Vedanta theologians.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: In the verses of volume 3, _____ asserts that life emerges through three routes: an egg, direct birth of a living being, and as life sprouting from seeds
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: In volume 2 Uddalaka, rejects the idea that the world was born from the non-existent [a-sat], asserting that "in the beginning this world was simply what is existent [sat]- one only, without a second." The existent thought "let me become many," emitting heat. In the verses of volume 3, Uddalaka asserts that life emerges through three routes: an egg, direct birth of a living being, and as life sprouting from seeds.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: In 8.1 to 6, after setting this foundation of premises, in 6.8.1 to 6.8.6, _____ states that heat, food, water, mind, breath and voice have ultimately the existent (sat) as their root
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: In 8.1 to 6, after setting this foundation of premises, in 6.8.1 to 6.8.6, Uddalaka states that heat, food, water, mind, breath and voice have ultimately the existent (sat) as their root.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: In the traditional interpretation, 6.8.7 then states that Sat, _____, Being is this root, it is the essence (atman), it is at the core of all living beings
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: While tat is traditionally interpreted as referring to either 'the existent' (sat) or 'finest essence' (animan), Brereton has argued that this is grammatically incorrect, and that the phrase, as explained by Olivelle, "does not establish the identity between the individual and the ultimate being (sat) but rather shows that Svetaketu lives in the same manner as all other creatures, that is, by means of an invisible and subtle essence," which is also the cause of his existence. In the tradition...

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: It is True, it is Real, it is the Self (atman), and _____, Śvetaketu
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: It is True, it is Real, it is the Self (atman), and Thou Art That, Śvetaketu.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The "_____" phrase is a Mahavakya, a statement which leads directly to knowledge of Brahman
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The "Tat Tvam Asi" phrase is a Mahavakya, a statement which leads directly to knowledge of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The inmost essence of all beings is same, the whole world is _____, One Reality, One Self
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The inmost essence of all beings is same, the whole world is One Truth, One Reality, One Self. Uddalaka states in volume 6.10 of the Upanishad, that there comes a time when all human beings and all creatures know not, "I am this one, I am that one", but realize that they are One Truth, One Reality, and the whole world is one Atman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Living beings are like trees, asserts the Upanishad, that bleed when struck and injured, yet the tree lives on with its _____ as resplendent as before
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The inmost essence of all beings is same, the whole world is One Truth, One Reality, One Self. Living beings are like rivers that arise in the mountains, states the Upanishad, some rivers flow to the east and some to the west, yet they end in an ocean, become the ocean itself, and realize they are not different but are same, and thus realize their Oneness.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: It is this _____, that despite all the suffering inflicted on a person, makes him to stand up again, live and rejoice at life
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Uddalaka states in volume 6.10 of the Upanishad, that there comes a time when all human beings and all creatures know not, "I am this one, I am that one", but realize that they are One Truth, One Reality, and the whole world is one Atman. It is this Atman, that despite all the suffering inflicted on a person, makes him to stand up again, live and rejoice at life.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The Sat is forever, and this Sat is the _____, the essence, it exists, it is true, asserts the text
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The Self and the body are like salt and water, states the Upanishad in volume 6.13. The Sat is forever, and this Sat is the Self, the essence, it exists, it is true, asserts the text.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: He then finds his way out of the forest, then finds knowledgeable ones for directions to _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Man's journey to self-knowledge and self-realization, states volume 6.14 of Chandogya Upanishad, is like a man who is taken from his home in Gandharas, with his eyes covered, into a forest full of life-threatening dangers and delicious fruits, but no human beings. He then finds his way out of the forest, then finds knowledgeable ones for directions to Gandharas.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The latter asks, "teach me, Sir, the knowledge of _____, because I hear that anyone who knows the Self, is beyond suffering and sorrow"
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The latter asks, "teach me, Sir, the knowledge of Self, because I hear that anyone who knows the Self, is beyond suffering and sorrow".

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Sanatkumara first inquires from _____ what he already has learned so far
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Sanatkumara first inquires from Narada what he already has learned so far. Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Narada admits to _____ that none of these have led him to Self-knowledge, and he wants to know about Self and Self-knowledge
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Sanatkumara first inquires from Narada what he already has learned so far. Narada admits to Sanatkumara that none of these have led him to Self-knowledge, and he wants to know about Self and Self-knowledge.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Narada admits to Sanatkumara that none of these have led him to Self-knowledge, and he wants to know about Self and Self-knowledge. Sanatkumara states that Narada, with the worldly knowledge, has so far focussed on name.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Narada admits to Sanatkumara that none of these have led him to Self-knowledge, and he wants to know about Self and Self-knowledge. Sanatkumara states that Narada, with the worldly knowledge, has so far focussed on name.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Deeper than this name, is speech asserts verse 7.2.1, because speech is what communicates all outer worldly knowledge as well as what is right and what is wrong, what is true and what is false, what is good and what is bad, what is pleasant and what is unpleasant. Without speech, men can't share this knowledge, and one must adore and revere speech as manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: One must adore and revere Mind as _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Without speech, men can't share this knowledge, and one must adore and revere speech as manifestation of Brahman. One must adore and revere Mind as Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: One must adore and revere Will as manifestation of _____
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: One must adore and revere Mind as Brahman. One must adore and revere Will as manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Higher than Will, states section 7.5 of the Upanishad, is _____ (चित्त, thought, consciousness) because when a man Thinks he forms his Will
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Higher than Will, states section 7.5 of the Upanishad, is Chitta (चित्त, thought, consciousness) because when a man Thinks he forms his Will.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: One must adore and revere Will as manifestation of Brahman. One must adore and revere Thought as manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Greater than Thought, asserts section 7.6 of the Upanishad, is Dhyanam (ध्यान, meditation, reflection, contemplation) because when a man Meditates he Thinks.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Greater than Thought, asserts section 7.6 of the Upanishad, is Dhyanam (ध्यान, meditation, reflection, contemplation) because when a man Meditates he Thinks. One must adore and revere Meditation as the manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Greater than Thought, asserts section 7.6 of the Upanishad, is Dhyanam (ध्यान, meditation, reflection, contemplation) because when a man Meditates he Thinks. One must adore and revere Meditation as the manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Deeper than Meditation, states section 7.7 of the Upanishad, is Vijñana (विज्ञान, knowledge, understanding, discernment) because when a man Understands he continues Meditating. One must adore and revere Understanding as the Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The text states in section 7.8, that higher than _____ is Bala (बल, strength, vigor) because a Strong man physically prevails over the men with Understanding
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Deeper than Meditation, states section 7.7 of the Upanishad, is Vijñana (विज्ञान, knowledge, understanding, discernment) because when a man Understands he continues Meditating. One must adore and revere Understanding as the Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Higher than _____, states section 7.9 of the Upanishad, is Anna (अन्नं, food, nourishment) because with proper Food, man becomes Strong
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The text states in section 7.8, that higher than Understanding is Bala (बल, strength, vigor) because a Strong man physically prevails over the men with Understanding. "By strength does the world stand", states verse 7.8.1 of Chandogya Upanishad.

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: One must adore and revere Strength as the manifestation of Brahman. One must adore and revere Food as manifestation of Brahman.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: One must adore and revere Water as the _____

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.fact: Higher than Water, asserts section 7.11 of the Upanishad, is Tejas (तेजस्, heat, fire) because it is Heat combined with Wind and Atmosphere that bring Rain Water.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: The text states in section 7.13, that deeper than Space is Smara (स्मरो, memory) because without _____ [U]niverse to man would be as if it did not exist
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The text states in section 7.13, that deeper than Space is Smara (स्मरो, memory) because without Memory [U]niverse to man would be as if it did not exist. One must adore and revere Memory as the manifestation of Brahman, states the text.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: One must adore and revere _____ as the manifestation of Brahman, states the text
Chandogya Upanishad.fact: The text states in section 7.13, that deeper than Space is Smara (स्मरो, memory) because without Memory [U]niverse to man would be as if it did not exist. One must adore and revere Memory as the manifestation of Brahman, states the text.

Chandogya Upanishad.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Chandogya Upanishad.question: Deeper than _____ is Asha (आशा, hope), states section 7.14 of the Upanishad, because kindled by Hope the Memory learns and man acts

Kali.fact: Parvati performs austerities to lose her dark complexion and becomes Gauri, the golden one.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: They soon find that they have worsened the situation for with every drop of blood that drips from _____īja, he reproduces a duplicate of himself
Kali.fact: They soon find that they have worsened the situation for with every drop of blood that drips from Raktabīja, he reproduces a duplicate of himself.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She has deep, red eyes with tongue lolling out as she catches drops of _____īja's blood before they fall to the ground and create duplicates
Kali.fact: She has deep, red eyes with tongue lolling out as she catches drops of Raktabīja's blood before they fall to the ground and create duplicates. Kali consumes Raktabīja and his duplicates, and dances on the corpses of the slain.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She is given the epithet Cāṃuṇḍā (_____), that is, the slayer of the demons Chanda and Munda
Kali.fact: She is given the epithet Cāṃuṇḍā (Chamunda), that is, the slayer of the demons Chanda and Munda. Chamunda is very often identified with Kali and is very much like her in appearance and habit.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: In both, she is described as being black in colour, though she is often seen as blue in popular _____ art
Kali.fact: In both, she is described as being black in colour, though she is often seen as blue in popular Indian art.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She is often depicted naked which symbolizes her being beyond the covering of Maya since she is pure (nirguna) being-consciousness-bliss and far above _____
Kali.fact: She is often depicted naked which symbolizes her being beyond the covering of Maya since she is pure (nirguna) being-consciousness-bliss and far above Prakriti.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She is shown as very dark as she is _____ in its supreme unmanifest state
Kali.fact: She is shown as very dark as she is Brahman in its supreme unmanifest state.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: There is no association with _____
Kali.fact: There is no association with Shiva.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: One version of the origin of her name comes from the story of _____, lord of death, who lives in the south (dakshina)
Kali.fact: One version of the origin of her name comes from the story of Yama, lord of death, who lives in the south (dakshina). When Yama heard Kali's name, he fled in terror, and so those who worship Kali are said to be able to overcome death itself.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She was unable to see beyond the limitless power of her rage and _____ had to move out of her way
Kali.fact: Vishnu confronted Kali in an attempt to cool her down. She was unable to see beyond the limitless power of her rage and Vishnu had to move out of her way.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: He was a noted 17th-century _____ thinker and author of Tantrasara
Kali.fact: He was a noted 17th-century Bengali Tantra thinker and author of Tantrasara.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She is worshipped by warriors, tantrics – the followers of _____
Kali.fact: She is worshipped by warriors, tantrics – the followers of Tantra.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: This can symbolize the letters of the _____ alphabet and therefore as the primordial sound of Aum from which all creation proceeds
Kali.fact: This can symbolize the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet and therefore as the primordial sound of Aum from which all creation proceeds.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: A common interpretation is that _____ symbolizes purusha, the universal unchanging aspect of reality, or pure consciousness
Kali.fact: There are several interpretations of the symbolism behind the commonly represented image of Kali standing on Shiva's supine form. A common interpretation is that Shiva symbolizes purusha, the universal unchanging aspect of reality, or pure consciousness.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: Consciousness and energy are dependent upon each other, since Shiva depends on _____, or energy, in order to fulfill his role in creation, preservation, and destruction
Kali.fact: Consciousness and energy are dependent upon each other, since Shiva depends on Shakti, or energy, in order to fulfill his role in creation, preservation, and destruction. In this view, without Shakti, Shiva is a corpse—unable to act.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: In this view, without _____, Shiva is a corpse—unable to act
Kali.fact: Consciousness and energy are dependent upon each other, since Shiva depends on Shakti, or energy, in order to fulfill his role in creation, preservation, and destruction. In this view, without Shakti, Shiva is a corpse—unable to act.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: As a result, goddesses play an important role in the study and practice of _____ and are essential in understanding the nature of reality
Kali.fact: As a result, goddesses play an important role in the study and practice of Tantra Yoga and are essential in understanding the nature of reality.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kali.fact: With the exception of being associated with Parvati as Shiva's consort, Kāli is rarely pictured in Hindu legends and iconography as a motherly figure until Bengali devotions beginning in the early eighteenth century. Even in Bengāli tradition her appearance and habits change little, if at all.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: In contrast, the _____ devotee adopts the attitude of a child, coming to love her unreservedly
Kali.fact: With the exception of being associated with Parvati as Shiva's consort, Kāli is rarely pictured in Hindu legends and iconography as a motherly figure until Bengali devotions beginning in the early eighteenth century. In contrast, the Bengali devotee adopts the attitude of a child, coming to love her unreservedly.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: A significant portion of _____ devotional music features Kāli as its central theme and is known as Shyama Sangeet
Kali.fact: A significant portion of Bengali devotional music features Kāli as its central theme and is called Shyama Sangeet.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kali.fact: The rituals in eastern India temples where animals are killed are generally led by Brahmin priests. A Brahmin priest will recite a mantra in the ear of the animal to be sacrificed, in order to free the animal from the cycle of life and death.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: Groups such as People for _____ continue to protest animal sacrifice based on court rulings forbidding the practice in some locations
Kali.fact: The rituals in eastern India temples where animals are killed are generally led by Brahmin priests. Groups such as People for Animals continue to protest animal sacrifice based on court rulings forbidding the practice in some locations.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She features as a key deity in the practice tradition of Chöd founded by _____ and is seen as a fierce form of Vajrayogini
Kali.fact: She features as a key deity in the practice tradition of Chöd set up by Machig Labdron and is seen as a fierce form of Vajrayogini.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: Other similar fierce deities include the dark blue _____ and the lion-faced Simhamukha
Kali.fact: Other similar fierce deities include the dark blue Ugra Tara and the lion-faced Simhamukha.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She is regarded as having seven forms; _____āli, Mahābhadrakāli, Pēnakāli, Vandurukāli (Hanumāpatrakāli), Rīrikāli, Sohonkāli, and Ginikāli
Kali.fact: She is regarded as having seven forms; Bhadrakāli, Mahābhadrakāli, Pēnakāli, Vandurukāli (Hanumāpatrakāli), Rīrikāli, Sohonkāli, and Ginikāli.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: Red flowers, silver coins, blood, and oil lamps with mustard oil are offered to her, and as _____'s servant, she accepts offerings on her behalf
Kali.fact: Red flowers, silver coins, blood, and oil lamps with mustard oil are offered to her, and as Pattini's servant, she accepts offerings on her behalf. Kali has been seen as both a demon (though a tamed one, thanks to Pattini) and a goddess in Sri Lanka.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: She and mythical _____ kings both use demonic fury as a necessary condition of conquest
Kali.fact: She and mythical Sinhala Buddhist kings both use demonic fury as a necessary condition of conquest.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: Yantras are used in relation to her, sourced from the _____, later Buddhist paritta chants, and from non-Buddhist yantras and mantras
Kali.fact: Yantras are used in relation to her, sourced from the Pali Canon, later Buddhist paritta chants, and from non-Buddhist yantras and mantras.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: The Sādhakayantra is popular, and its corresponding mantra includes Arabic words and _____ concepts
Kali.fact: The Sādhakayantra is popular, and its corresponding mantra includes Arabic words and Islamic concepts.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: By _____, she amended this view stating that cross-cultural borrowing should be done thoughtfully and is natural due to religious globalization
Kali.fact: By 2003, she amended this view stating that cross-cultural borrowing should be done thoughtfully and is natural due to religious globalization.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: The Malbars have Tamil ancestry but are, at least nominally, _____
Kali.fact: The Malbars have Tamil ancestry but are, at least nominally, Catholics.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: In the Beatles' _____ film Help!, Ringo Starr is pursued by Kali worshippers intending to sacrifice him
Kali.fact: In the Beatles' 1965 film Help!, Ringo Starr is pursued by Kali worshippers intending to sacrifice him.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: A modern version of Kali was featured on the cover of the first issue of feminist magazine Ms., published in _____, with Kali's arms symbolizing the many tasks of the contemporary American woman
Kali.fact: A modern version of Kali was featured on the cover of the first issue of feminist magazine Ms., published in 1972, with Kali's arms symbolizing the many tasks of the contemporary American woman.

Kali.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kali.question: The tongue and lips logo of the band The Rolling Stones, created in _____, was inspired by the stuck-out tongue of Kali
Kali.fact: The tongue and lips logo of the band The Rolling Stones, created in 1971, was inspired by the stuck-out tongue of Kali.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: The _____ was Hindu god of love.
Kamadeva.fact: Kamadeva (Sanskrit: कामदेव, IAST: Kāmadeva), also called Kama, Manmatha, and Madana is the Hindu god of love, attraction, pleasure and beauty, as well as the personification of the concept of kāma. Kamadeva's origins are traced to the verses of the Rig Veda and Atharva Veda, although he is better known from the stories of the Puranas.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: He is often portrayed alongside his consort and female counterpart, _____
Kamadeva.fact: He is often portrayed alongside his consort and female counterpart, Rati.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: His most popular myth is his incineration by the god Shiva's third eye and rebirth on earth as _____, the eldest son of Krishna and his chief consort Rukmini
Kamadeva.fact: His most popular myth is his incineration by the god Shiva's third eye and rebirth on earth as Pradyumna, the eldest son of Krishna and his chief consort Rukmini.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: Deva means heavenly or divine and refers to a deity in _____
Kamadeva.fact: Deva means heavenly or divine and refers to a deity in Hinduism.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: Kama (_____: kāma) means "passion" or "longing", especially as in sensual or passionate love
Kamadeva.fact: Kama (IAST: kāma) means "passion" or "longing", especially as in sensual or passionate love.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: The name is used in the _____ (RV 9, 113
Kamadeva.fact: The name is used in the Rigveda (RV 9, 113.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: It is also a name of the deities _____ and Shiva
Kamadeva.fact: It is also a name of the deities Krishna and Shiva.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kamadeva.fact: Kama is also a name used for Agni (Atharva Veda 6.36.3).

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: John Muir notes that _____ in the Vedas does not refer to the sexual desire, but rather desire of goodness in general
Kamadeva.fact: Kama is also a name used for Agni (Atharva Veda 6.36.3). These early Vedic texts reflect the formative stages of Kamadeva’s mythological identity.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: In Rigveda 10.129, often referred to as the _____ or the Hymn of Creation, kāma emerges as a primordial force central to the cosmogonic process
Kamadeva.fact: In Rigveda 10.129, often called the Nasadiya Sukta or the Hymn of Creation, kāma emerges as a primordial force central to the cosmogonic process.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: In the _____, Kāma begins to take on a more defined, divine character
Kamadeva.fact: In the Atharvaveda, Kāma begins to take on a more defined, divine character.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: The deity is described with titles such as “first seed of mind” (manoja, mind-born one), echoing his _____ origins
Kamadeva.fact: The deity is described with titles such as “first seed of mind” (manoja, mind-born one), echoing his Rigvedic origins.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: According to _____ of the Lake Forest College (Department of Religion), this form of Kāma is simultaneously a divine agent of desire and a god with cosmic significance
Kamadeva.fact: According to Professor Catherine Benton of the Lake Forest College (Department of Religion), this form of Kāma is simultaneously a divine agent of desire and a god with cosmic significance.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: Hymn 19.52 of the _____ continues this theme, offering homage to Kāma as a bestower of prosperity and success, likely in connection with sacrificial rites
Kamadeva.fact: Hymn 19.52 of the Atharvaveda continues this theme, offering homage to Kāma as a bestower of prosperity and success, likely in connection with sacrificial rites. A significant shift toward the later mythological depiction of Kamadeva appears in Atharvaveda 3.25.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: Again, Kāma is described as “the first seed of mind,” indicating continuity with the _____ view of desire as a force foundational to creation
Kamadeva.fact: Again, Kāma is described as “the first seed of mind,” indicating continuity with the Rigvedic view of desire as a force foundational to creation.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: This hymn illustrates Kāma in a form more closely resembling the god portrayed in the epics and _____
Kamadeva.fact: This hymn illustrates Kāma in a form more closely resembling the god portrayed in the epics and Puranas.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: While 20th-century scholar A. _____ considered the text reflective of the "lower side" of religious life, contemporary scholars emphasize its appeal across all societal strata
Kamadeva.fact: While 20th-century scholar A. Berriedale Keith considered the text reflective of the "lower side" of religious life, contemporary scholars emphasize its appeal across all societal strata.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: According to _____, although some stories in the Brahmanas touch on themes of sexual pleasure, these do not establish kāma as a divine being
Kamadeva.fact: According to Benton, although some stories in the Brahmanas touch on themes of sexual pleasure, these do not establish kāma as a divine being. A notable verse in the fourth khaṇḍa of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa—closely echoing Atharvaveda 3.29.7—states: “Desire has given to desire; desire is the giver, desire the receiver.” Although this formulaic expression may suggest a symbolic exchange involving kāma, Benton cautions that it should not be read as e.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kamadeva.fact: John Dowson, however, states that in the Taittiriya Brahmana, Kama appears as a deity, described as the son of deities Dharma (righteousness personified) and Shraddha (faith personified).

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: The epic often portrays victims of desire as struck by “the sharp arrows of _____,” emphasizing the emotional and psychological impact of passion
Kamadeva.fact: The epic often portrays victims of desire as struck by “the sharp arrows of Manmatha,” emphasizing the emotional and psychological impact of passion.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: For instance, the princess Amba is described as tormented by Kāma’s arrow when rejected by beloved Shalva (_____ 5.172.8)
Kamadeva.fact: Philosophy and mythology blend throughout the Mahabharata in depictions of Kamadeva. For instance, the princess Amba is described as tormented by Kāma’s arrow when rejected by beloved Shalva (Mahabharata 5.172.8).

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kamadeva.fact: The Udyoga Parva locates Kāma in the northern direction, the domain of Shiva and Uma (Parvati) at Mount Kailash.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Kamadeva.fact: In one passage, the warrior Ashvatthama is described as born from parts of Shiva, Yama (Death), Kama, and Krodha, embodying desire, rage, and destruction.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: This marks the emergence of the epithet _____ (“the bodiless one”) and symbolizes the conflict between ascetic detachment and sensual desire
Kamadeva.fact: This marks the emergence of the epithet Ananga (“the bodiless one”) and symbolizes the conflict between ascetic detachment and sensual desire.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: Bhishma lists Kāma among seven such cosmic sustainers, including _____ and Time
Kamadeva.fact: Bhishma lists Kāma among seven such cosmic sustainers, including Dharma and Time.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: This passage preserves an older _____ conception of desire not merely as a temptation but as a generative and sustaining principle
Kamadeva.fact: This passage preserves an older Vedic conception of desire not merely as a temptation but as a generative and sustaining principle.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: He is known for his power to disturb minds and kindle longing, attributes evident in his epithets: _____ (“mind-disturber”) and Madana (“intoxicator”)
Kamadeva.fact: He is known for his power to disturb minds and kindle longing, attributes evident in his epithets: Manmatha (“mind-disturber”) and Madana (“intoxicator”).

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: After his wife _____'s abduction, Rama is described as being overcome by longing and mental distress
Kamadeva.fact: After his wife Sita's abduction, Rama is described as being overcome by longing and mental distress.

Kamadeva.fact: In early scriptures, including the Taittiriya Brahmana and the Mahabharata, Kamadeva is described as the son of Dharma, the personification of righteousness and a Prajāpati (progenitor deity). Kama's mother is mentioned to be Dharma's wife Shraddha in Taittiriya Brahmana, while the appendix of the Mahabharata, Harivamsa, states his mother to be Lakshmi, another wife of Dharma.

Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Kamadeva.question: According to _____ scriptures including the Shiva Purana, the Kalika Purana, the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, and the Matsya Purana, Kama is one of the mind-born sons of the creator god Brahma
Kamadeva.fact: According to Puranic scriptures including the Shiva Purana, the Kalika Purana, the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, and the Matsya Purana, Kama is one of the mind-born sons of the creator god Brahma.

Kamadeva.fact: According to Puranic scriptures including the Shiva Purana, the Kalika Purana, the Brahma Vaivarta Purana, and the Matsya Purana, Kama is one of the mind-born sons of the creator god Brahma. Kamadeva.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Parvati.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Parvati.question: The _____ was Major goddess in Hinduism.
Parvati.fact: Parvati (Sanskrit: पार्वती, IAST: Pārvatī), also called Uma (Sanskrit: उमा, IAST: Umā) and Gauri (Sanskrit: गौरी, IAST: Gaurī), is one of the principal goddesses in Hinduism, revered as the goddess of power, energy, nourishment, harmony, love, beauty, devotion, and motherhood. From her first appearance as a goddess during the epic period (400 BCE – 400 CE), Parvati is primarily depicted as the consort of the god Shiva.

Parvati.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Parvati.question: Along with _____ and Sarasvati, she forms the trinity, known as the Tridevi
Parvati.fact: Along with Lakshmi and Sarasvati, she forms the trinity, called the Tridevi.

Parvati.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Parvati.subject: Hinduism & Mythology
Parvati.question: She is the source of power that energises _____, who without her is incomplete
Parvati.fact: Philosophically, Parvati is regarded as Shiva’s shakti (divine energy or power), the personification of the creative force that sustains the cosmos. She is the source of power that energises Shiva, who without her is incomplete.

Parvati.subject: Hinduism & Mythology

Parvati.fact: In various Shaiva traditions, Parvati is also regarded as a model devotee, and even viewed as the embodiment of Shiva's grace, playing a central role in the spiritual liberation of devotees. In Hindu temples dedicated to her and Shiva, she is symbolically represented as the yoni.

Parvati.fact: She is also the ferocious Mahakali that wields a sword, wears a garland of severed heads, and protects her devotees and destroys all evil that plagues the world and its beings.
